stories.title: The Berlin Wall separated his family. Its legacy still endures
stories.summary: This feature is the first in a series examining how artificial borders reshape daily life, divide families and force loved ones to navigate the human cost of political geography. Erich Guetinger was 18 years old when he first saw his uncle’s family as an adult. Having last seen them as a small child, Guetinger was both excited and nervous to see his uncle, aunt, and two older cousins after so long. It was the summer of 1969 – the Beatles were recording Abbey Road, the United States had begun withdrawing troops from Vietnam, and Neil Armstrong was about to become the first person to walk on the moon. By then, Germany had been divided for two decades. The Federal Republic of Germany, or West Germany, was a capitalist democracy aligned with the US and Western Europe. The German Democratic Republic, or East Germany, was a Soviet-aligned socialist state governed by the Socialist Unity Party. Berlin itself had been divided since 1945, and the construction of the Berlin Wall in 1961 had hardened that separation. The two states differed sharply in size and population. About 51 million people lived in West Germany and about 18 million in East Germany, separated by a nearly 2,000km (1,242 miles) border running from the Baltic Sea to the Czechoslovak border. By 1969, West Germany’s population had grown to about 61 million, while East Germany’s had fallen to roughly 17 million. With most of his family in their hometown of Babenhausen, Bavaria, and his uncle Hans, aunt Frieda, and cousins Dieter and Guenter in Brieskow-Finkenheerd, a village near Frankfurt an der Oder in East Germany, the Guetingers were directly affected by Germany’s political partition.

stories.title: Four-legged lifesavers: Inside South Korea’s growing canine blood donation network
stories.summary: Cappu is seven years old, weighs 31kg and, by most measures, lives an ordinary golden retriever’s life. But over the past four years, he has quietly built up an unusual record: 10 blood donations. His latest and final donation came on July 31 at Konkuk University’s KU I’m Dognor Blood Donation Center in Gwangjin-gu, Seoul. By then, Cappu had collected the full set of colourful scarves the centre gives canine donors as they mark each donation milestone. For his guardian, Jo Hang-deok, the idea of having a dog donate blood was not something he had initially considered. “I knew that dogs can sometimes need blood transfusions, but I did not know much about the fact that companion dogs could actually participate in blood donation themselves,” Jo told. The Korea Herald on Aug 19. “I happened to learn about canine blood donation and decided to participate because I thought Cappu could help other dogs.” Cappu is part of a still-small but growing effort to change how canine blood is supplied in South Korea in recent years. Unlike the human blood supply, which is supported by a nationwide system driven by organisations such as the Korean Red Cross, canine blood remains far more fragmented. Individual veterinary hospitals differ in their ability to collect and store blood, while access to outside suppliers also varies. Donated blood must be tested and stored properly, and its limited shelf life makes it impossible for hospitals simply to stockpile large quantities indefinitely.
